---
title: "Syntax"
---

A working reference for Jestyr's surface syntax.

**Every numbered block on this page is a complete program**, and the output
shown under it is the real output of running that program with the current
compiler — not an illustration. Copy any block into `demo.jtr` and run it:

```bash
cargo run -- run demo.jtr        # or:  ./jc demo.jtr run
```

Files use the `.jtr` extension. Comments are `//` (doc comments are `///`,
collected by `jestyrc doc`). Statements end at newlines — no semicolons.

## 1. Bindings and primitive types

```{.rust}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let x: i32 = 42          // immutable binding
    var y: i64 = -5          // mutable binding
    y = y + 1

    let n: usize = 10        // sizes and indices
    let f: f64 = 2.5
    let ok: bool = true
    let s: str = "a view"    // a borrowed string view

    print_int(x)
    print_int(y)
    print_int(n as i64)      // conversions are explicit: `as`
    print_float(f)
    print_int(ok as i64)
    print_str(s)
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
42
-4
10
2.5
1
a view
:::

Integer types are `i32`, `i64`, `u8`, `u64`, `usize` and friends; floating
point is `f64` under a [locked determinism contract](determinism.qmd).

## 2. Functions and parameter conventions

The default parameter convention is `read` — an immutable borrow. `mut`
borrows exclusively, and only `take` transfers ownership. That is the whole
ownership surface most code ever sees (see [Safety](safety.qmd)). Contracts
ride on the signature and lower to checked asserts.

```{.rust}
struct Rect { w: i64, h: i64 }

fn area(read r: Rect) -> i64 { return r.w * r.h }   // borrow (the default)
fn grow(mut r: Rect) { r.w = r.w * 2 }              // exclusive borrow

fn clamp(x: i32, lo: i32, hi: i32) -> i32
    requires lo <= hi
    ensures result >= lo
{
    if x < lo { return lo }
    if x > hi { return hi }
    return x
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    var r: Rect = Rect { w: 3, h: 4 }
    print_int(area(r))
    grow(r)
    print_int(area(r))
    print_int(clamp(99, 0, 10) as i64)
    print_int(clamp(-99, 0, 10) as i64)
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
12
24
10
0
:::

## 3. Control flow

`for` is the single unified loop: condition loops, ranges, and element loops
are all spelled with it. Loop bindings take the same conventions as
parameters — `read x` borrows each element, `mut x` mutates in place.

```{.rust}
fn main() -> i32 {
    let a: i32 = -5
    var b: i32 = 0
    if a < -1 { b = 1 } else if a == 0 { b = 2 } else { b = 3 }
    print_int(b as i64)

    var i: i32 = 0
    for i < 3 { i = i + 1 }          // while-style: for <condition>
    print_int(i as i64)

    var total: i64 = 0
    for k in 0..5 { total = total + k }   // range (0..=5 includes the end)
    print_int(total)

    var xs: [3]i32 = [10, 20, 30]
    for read x in xs { print_int(x as i64) }   // borrow each element
    for mut x in xs { x = x + 1 }              // mutate in place
    print_int(xs[0] as i64)
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
1
3
10
10
20
30
11
:::

`for { … }` loops forever with `break`/`continue`; a search loop can carry an
`else` that runs when it finds nothing (`examples/loops_else.jtr`).

## 4. Structs, enums, and `match`

Match exhaustiveness is checked: add a variant and every `match` over the
enum becomes a compile error until it is handled.

```{.rust}
struct Point { x: i64, y: i64 }

enum Shape {
    circle(r: i64),
    rect(w: i64, h: i64),
    empty,
}

fn area(read s: Shape) -> i64 {
    match s {
        circle(r)  => 3 * r * r,
        rect(w, h) => w * h,
        empty      => 0,
    }
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let p: Point = Point { x: 3, y: 4 }
    let q: Point = Point { x: 9, ..p }   // struct update / spread
    print_int(p.x)
    print_int(q.x)
    print_int(q.y)
    print_int(area(circle(2)))
    print_int(area(rect(3, 5)))
    print_int(area(empty))
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
3
9
4
12
15
0
:::

Recursive enums box their children explicitly — Jestyr never hides an
allocation:

```{.rust}
enum Expr {
    lit(v: i32),
    add(l: indirect Expr, r: indirect Expr),
}
```

`match` also supports guards, or-patterns and rest-patterns
(`examples/{guards,orpat,rest_pat}.jtr`). `distinct UserId = i32` makes a
zero-cost newtype that will not interconvert silently; `record` declares
immutable-by-construction values.

## 5. Arrays, strings, slices

A fixed array is a stack **value** — it copies, passes and returns by value.
Indexing is bounds-checked (checks elide only under a refinement proof, see
`examples/refine.jtr`). `str` borrows; `String` owns.

```{.rust}
fn main() -> i32 {
    var board: [8]i32 = [0; 8]
    board[3] = 1
    print_int(board[3] as i64)

    var owned: String = string_from("Hello")
    string_push(owned, ", world")
    print_str(string_view(owned))   // lend the buffer as a view, no copy
    print_int(owned.len as i64)
    string_free(owned)

    for w in split("a,bb,ccc", ",") { print_int(w.len as i64) }  // zero-copy
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
1
Hello, world
12
1
2
3
:::

A slice `[]T` is a fat-pointer view over contiguous memory:

```{.rust}
fn seti(p: *mut i64, i: usize, v: i64) { unsafe { (p + i).* = v } }

fn total(read s: []i64) -> i64 {
    var acc: i64 = 0
    for x in s { acc = acc + x }
    return acc
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    var a: *mut i64 = alloc(i64, 4)
    seti(a, 0, 10)
    seti(a, 1, 20)
    seti(a, 2, 30)
    seti(a, 3, 40)
    let s: []i64 = slice(i64, a, 4)
    print_int(s.len as i64)
    print_int(s[2])
    print_int(total(s))
    free_ptr(a)
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
4
30
100
:::

## 6. Errors: sets, payloads, `?`, `catch`

Error sets are part of the signature and checked through every call and `?`
hop. An error name can carry one payload value, stack-only — no allocation,
no dynamic dispatch.

```{.rust}
fn parse(n: i64) -> i64 !{ Empty, TooBig(i64) } {
    if n == 0  { return err(Empty) }
    if n > 99  { return err(TooBig(n)) }   // the payload rides along
    return ok(n * 2)
}

fn hop(n: i64) -> i64 !{ Empty, TooBig(i64) } {
    let v = parse(n)?              // propagate; set inclusion is checked
    return ok(v + 1)
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    print_int(hop(5) catch 0 - 1)  // a plain default
    print_int(hop(500) catch |e| match e { Empty => 0 - 1, TooBig(v) => v })
    print_int(hop(0)   catch |e| match e { Empty => 0 - 1, TooBig(v) => v })
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
11
500
-1
:::

The `500` is the payload: it was created deep inside `parse`, crossed a `?`
hop untouched, and was extracted by name at the top. Error sets work in trait
signatures too (next section), and `--error-traces` records the propagation
path.

## 7. Generics and traits

Bounds are checked at the definition site and monomorphized — no vtable, no
allocation. `dyn Trait` opts into dynamic dispatch where you want it.

```{.rust}
struct Checking { balance: i64 }
struct Savings { balance: i64, reserve: i64 }

trait Account {
    fn withdraw(read self, amt: i64) -> i64 !{ Insufficient(i64) }
}

impl Account for Checking {
    fn withdraw(read self, amt: i64) -> i64 !{ Insufficient(i64) } {
        if amt > self.balance { return err(Insufficient(self.balance)) }
        return ok(self.balance - amt)
    }
}

impl Account for Savings {
    fn withdraw(read self, amt: i64) -> i64 !{ Insufficient(i64) } {
        let avail: i64 = self.balance - self.reserve
        if amt > avail { return err(Insufficient(avail)) }
        return ok(self.balance - amt)
    }
}

fn spend[T: Account](read acct: T, amt: i64) -> i64 {   // bounded generic
    return acct.withdraw(amt) catch |e| match e {
        Insufficient(avail) => 0 - avail,
    }
}

fn dup[T](take x: T) -> T { return x }                   // unbounded

fn main() -> i32 {
    let c: Checking = Checking { balance: 100 }
    let s: Savings = Savings { balance: 100, reserve: 80 }
    print_int(spend(c, 30))
    print_int(spend(s, 30))
    print_int(dup(7))
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
70
-20
7
:::

The `-20` is the savings account refusing: only 20 was spendable above its
reserve, and the error carried that number back through the trait call.

## 8. References beyond borrows

Two tiers exist for references that must be *stored*: `genref` (checked at
every deref) and `region` (checked by scope, free at runtime). See
[Safety](safety.qmd) for when to reach for which.

```{.rust}
struct Point { x: i64, y: i64 }

fn main() -> i32 {
    var r: &i32 = gen_new(i32, 42)   // {pointer, generation}
    print_int(r.* as i64)            // deref checks the generation
    gen_free(r)                       // a later deref would FAULT, not corrupt

    region a {
        var p: &[a]Point = region_alloc(a, Point, Point { x: 1, y: 2 })
        var q: &[a]Point = region_alloc(a, Point, Point { x: 10, y: 20 })
        print_int(p.*.x)              // plain pointer deref — no check
        print_int(q.*.y)
    }                                 // whole arena freed here, O(1)
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
42
1
20
:::

Returning a `&[a]T` out of its `region` block is a compile error
(`examples/region_escape.jtr`).

## 9. Concurrency and parallelism

`concurrent` is a nursery: every task spawned inside it is joined at the
closing brace, so no task outlives its scope.

```{.rust}
fn worker(c: *mut i64) { atomic_add(c, 1) }

fn main() -> i32 {
    var c: *mut i64 = alloc(i64, 1)
    atomic_store(c, 0)
    concurrent {
        spawn worker(c)
        spawn worker(c)
        spawn worker(c)
        spawn worker(c)
    }
    print_int(atomic_load(c))   // 4, whatever the interleaving
    free_ptr(c)
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
4
:::

Data parallelism is a reduction expression, and the reduction must come from
a declared-deterministic set:

```{.rust}
@span(log) fn par_sum_sq(read s: []i64) -> i64 {
    par for x in s reduce(core.sum_reduction()) { x * x }
}
```

A non-deterministic reduction is a compile error, and serializing a `par for`
back to a plain `for` violates the `@span` contract — also a compile error.
Channels, `select`, task handles with `await` and dynamic spawn counts round
out the surface (`examples/std/{channel,select,await}.jtr`); the full
[parallel reduction example](tour.qmd) shows it at scale.

## 10. Compile-time evaluation

A `comptime` block is evaluated while compiling and replaced by its value —
the emitted C contains only the answer.

```{.rust}
const SIZE: i64 = 8

fn fact(n: i64) -> i64 {
    if n <= 1 { return 1 }
    return n * fact(n - 1)
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let a: i64 = comptime { 2 + 2 }
    let b: i64 = comptime { fact(10) }   // recursion, at compile time
    let c: i64 = comptime { SIZE * 4 }
    print_int(a)
    print_int(b)
    print_int(c)
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
4
3628800
32
:::

The evaluator is total: step budgets and a call-depth cap turn a runaway
definition into a diagnostic rather than a hung build.

## 11. `unsafe`, raw pointers, and C interop

Raw pointers (`*mut T`, `*const T`) exist for FFI, MMIO and allocator
internals. Every dereference must sit inside an `unsafe` block — outside one
it is a compile error, on both toolchains.

```{.rust}
extern "c" fn abs(x: i32) -> i32      // C interop by bare name

fn main() -> i32 {
    var p: *mut i32 = alloc(i32, 4)
    unsafe { (p + 2).* = 7 }
    let v: i32 = unsafe { (p + 2).* }
    print_int(v as i64)
    free_ptr(p)
    print_int(abs(0 - 42) as i64)
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
7
42
:::

The obligations a raw pointer carries — validity, provenance, aliasing — are
written down in
[the unsafe contract](https://github.com/AdamEzzat1/Jestyr/blob/master/docs/unsafe-contract.md).

## 12. Attributes

These are declaration decorations rather than standalone programs; each links
to a runnable example.

| attribute | meaning |
|---|---|
| `@no_alloc` | proven allocation-free, transitively — a violation is a compile error |
| `@span(log)` / `@span(linear)` | checked work-span cost class |
| `@simd` | checked vectorization legality |
| `@deterministic` | rejects non-deterministic reductions |
| `@packed`, `@align(n)`, `@layout(auto)` | memory layout control |
| `@volatile`, `@address(0x…)` | bare-metal and MMIO |
| `@test`, `@bench` | the built-in harness (`jestyrc test`) |

See [the attributes doc](https://github.com/AdamEzzat1/Jestyr/blob/master/docs/attributes.md)
for the full catalogue with its compile-error examples, and the
[primes program](tour.qmd) for `@no_alloc` and contracts working together.

## 13. Modules

Module declarations need more than one file, so this section shows the forms
rather than a single runnable block; `examples/modules/` is the working
program.

```{.rust}
import "../std/mem"                 // path import
import "helpers" as h               // alias
import "vendored" = "3f9c…"         // pinned to a content hash

let a: Allocator = mem.system_allocator()   // qualified access
```

`pub` controls visibility, a directory can be a module, and the module graph
is content-hashed so it can be pinned like a lockfile. The self-hosted
compiler loads its own ten-module closure through exactly this system.
